The Evidence Room

Perjury & Section 340 Judgments

Rulings on false affidavits and false evidence in court, and on the procedure for prosecuting them under Section 340 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (now Section 379 BNSS).

24 judgments · 9 from the Supreme Court · updated 25 November 2026

Filing a false affidavit or giving false evidence in court is a criminal offence. Under Section 340 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, now Section 379 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, the court where it happened can make a written complaint to a magistrate, after a preliminary inquiry if it considers one necessary.

In family cases this most often arises when a party conceals income, employment or earlier proceedings to win or resist maintenance. The judgments here cover when a false statement is serious enough to prosecute (a deliberate false assertion, not a mere contradiction), the order in which a Section 340 application must be heard, time limits for deciding it, and costs for delay.

Perjury / §340 Allahabad High Court
Ranjeet Singh v. Neetu Singh
April 2026

Husband held disentitled to maintenance under Section 144 BNSS for concealing an existing HMA maintenance award and filing false financial affidavits — called it ‘economic abuse’ and imposed ₹15 lakh in compensatory costs.

Perjury / §340 Kerala High Court
Mohammed Nazer M.P. & Ors. v. Union Territory of Lakshadweep & Ors.
December 23, 2022

The High Court found prima facie that a Chief Judicial Magistrate had forged an investigating officer’s evidence during a criminal trial, and directed an inquiry under §195/340 CrPC and the magistrate’s suspension pending inquiry.

PRECEDENT Read Full Judgment →
Perjury / §340 P&H High Court
Smt. Ritu @ Ridhima & Anr. v. Sandeep Singh Sangwan
March 15, 2022

Upheld a perjury inquiry against a wife who falsely claimed no income in a maintenance plea despite earning roughly ₹28,000/month as an Assistant Professor — false assertions in court ‘undermine the dignity and sanctity of the court.’

PRECEDENT Read Full Judgment →
Perjury / §340 Supreme Court
State of Punjab v. Jasbir Singh
2022

Three-judge bench: a court acting on a §340 CrPC perjury complaint is not obliged to hold a preliminary inquiry or hear the would-be accused first.

Abhishek Dubey v. Archana Tiwari

Directed §340 CrPC proceedings after finding the petitioner had given a knowingly false residential address to the trial court.

Directed that a pending §340/§195 application be decided within two months, echoing the same expectation of timely disposal.

Perjury / §340 Bombay High Court
Electra Menezes v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
January 17, 2019

Directed that a pending §340/§195 application be decided within two months.

Perjury / §340 Bombay High Court
Fareed Ahmed Qureshi v. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
March 7, 2018

Found a prima facie case for a §340 complaint after a party made statements to the court that contradicted the official record and omitted material facts.

Perjury / §340 Bombay High Court
Union of India & Ors. v. Haresh Virumal Milani
April 17, 2017

Held that a §340 application must be decided before the main suit proceeds, and the prospective accused need not be heard before the preliminary inquiry is initiated.

Perjury / §340 Supreme Court
Amarsang Nathaji v. Hardik Harshadbhai Patel & Ors.
November 23, 2016

Set aside a High Court order initiating §340 proceedings, holding a mere contradictory statement is not enough — courts must independently find both a prima facie case and that prosecution is expedient in the interest of justice before ordering a perjury complaint.

Perjury / §340 Delhi High Court
HS Bedi v. National Highway Authority of India
January 22, 2016

Reiterated that dishonestly making a false claim before a court is independently punishable under IPC §209.

Perjury / §340 Bombay High Court
CTR Manufacturing Industries Ltd. v. Sergi Transformer Explosion Prevention Technologies Pvt. Ltd.
October 23, 2015

Found a prima facie case for perjury after a party withheld from the court that it had shared engineering drawings despite a subsisting injunction; the ruling was later reversed by the Supreme Court in 2016 for lack of the requisite criminal intent.

Perjury / §340 Delhi High Court
Sanjeev Kumar Mittal v. The State
November 18, 2010

Held that where prima facie perjury or forgery material exists but further evidence is beyond a private litigant’s reach, the court may direct a police investigation before formal §340 proceedings.

Held courts should impose heavy costs on a party using dilatory tactics to delay a §340 CrPC application.

Kenneth Desa & Anr. v. Gopal

Held that once a §340 application is filed, it must be registered for judicial inquiry — courts have little discretion to simply refuse to adjudicate it.

Using these judgments

Official Court Copy opens the judgment PDF from the Supreme Court’s own website. Full Judgment opens the complete judgment text (Indian Kanoon, or a PDF copy of the order). Read Report opens a news or legal-blog summary where no full text is linked yet.

To rely on a judgment in court, cite it by its case number or citation; the court’s registry can issue a certified copy. Check that it has not been overturned or modified on appeal. The one-line summaries on this page are for information only and are not legal advice.
